title: Shor's Algorithm — Integer Factoring
description: Peter Shor's 1994 algorithm factors large integers in polynomial time on a quantum computer by reducing factoring to order-finding, which quantum phase estimation solves exponentially faster than any known classical method. It threatens RSA cryptography directly: a large enough fault-tolerant quantum computer could factor the 2048-bit moduli that secure the modern internet. The algorithm is the reason post-quantum cryptography standardization is underway now, decades before the hardware exists.

If r even: factors = gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, N)

title: Grover's Search — Quadratic Speedup
description: Lov Grover's 1996 algorithm searches an unstructured database of N items in about √N steps instead of N/2, a provable quadratic speedup. It works by amplitude amplification: an oracle marks the target state and the diffusion operator rotates the state vector toward it, with the optimal iteration count near (π/4)√N. Applications include brute-force key search (halving effective symmetric-key strength), constraint satisfaction, and as a subroutine inside larger quantum algorithms.

title: VQE — Variational Quantum Eigensolver
description: The variational quantum eigensolver finds molecular ground-state energies by preparing a parameterized trial state on the quantum processor and letting a classical optimizer tune the parameters to minimize measured energy. Because only shallow circuits are needed, VQE runs on today's noisy devices and has computed dissociation curves for H2, LiH, and BeH2. It is the flagship near-term quantum chemistry algorithm and the template for the whole variational algorithm family.

title: QAOA — Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
description: Farhi's QAOA attacks combinatorial optimization — Max-Cut, scheduling, portfolio problems — by alternating a cost Hamiltonian that encodes the problem with a mixing Hamiltonian, tuned by 2p classical parameters for p layers. At p=1 it already beats random guessing on Max-Cut; deeper circuits approach the optimum as p grows. It runs natively on gate-model hardware and maps directly onto quantum annealers' problem class.

title: Quantum Phase Estimation
description: Quantum phase estimation extracts the eigenvalue phase of a unitary operator to n bits of precision using n ancilla qubits and the inverse quantum Fourier transform — it is the engine inside Shor's algorithm and quantum chemistry. Precision scales as 2^-n with n ancillas, and the algorithm succeeds with probability at least 4/π² ≈ 0.405 per run, boosted by repetition. Nearly every exponential quantum speedup traces back to this one subroutine.

title: Quantum Simulation of Molecules
description: Richard Feynman proposed in 1982 that quantum systems can only be efficiently simulated by quantum computers, and chemistry is the killer app: catalysts, batteries, and nitrogen fixation all hinge on electron correlation that defeats classical methods. Every percentage point of catalyst efficiency gained this way would move global energy use.

title: BB84 Quantum Key Distribution
description: Bennett and Brassard's 1984 protocol distributes encryption keys with security guaranteed by quantum physics: Alice sends qubits in random bases, Bob measures in random bases, and they keep only the bits where bases matched. Any eavesdropper disturbs the quantum states and reveals herself in the error rate. Real QKD networks operate today — metropolitan fiber links in China, Europe, and the US, plus satellite QKD via China's Micius satellite over 1,200 km.

title: Quantum Random Number Generation
description: Quantum random number generators harvest true randomness from quantum measurement — photon arrival times, beam-splitter paths, vacuum fluctuations — rather than deterministic algorithms. Commercial QRNG chips now ship in phones and HSMs, and device-independent protocols can certify randomness even from untrusted hardware via Bell-test violations. Every cryptographic key, lottery, and Monte Carlo simulation is only as unpredictable as its random source.

title: Quantum Machine Learning
description: Quantum machine learning explores whether quantum processors can learn patterns classical models cannot — through quantum kernels that compute classically-intractable feature maps, variational classifiers trained like neural nets, and quantum convolutional networks. Honest status: no proven broad advantage yet on real datasets, but quantum kernels have shown advantage on engineered problems, and the field is where neural nets were in the 1980s. PennyLane and TensorFlow Quantum are the standard playgrounds.

Annealing is the most qubit-rich quantum hardware in existence, and hybrid solvers now blend it with classical compute in the cloud.

title: Quantum Error Correction — Surface Code
description: Quantum error correction protects fragile qubits by spreading one logical qubit across many physical ones; the surface code tiles them on a 2D grid and corrects errors by measuring local parity checks called stabilizers. Below a threshold error rate (~1%), larger code distance suppresses logical errors exponentially — the path from noisy devices to fault tolerance. Google, IBM, and others have demonstrated distance-3 to distance-7 logical qubits with error suppression improving as distance grows.

title: Quantum Teleportation Protocol
description: Quantum teleportation moves an unknown quantum state from Alice to Bob using a shared entangled pair plus two classical bits — no matter transmitted, no faster-than-light signaling, and the original is destroyed per the no-cloning theorem. Bennett et al. proposed it in 1993; it has since been demonstrated over 1,400 km via satellite and across metropolitan fiber. Teleportation is the primitive behind quantum repeaters and distributed quantum computing.

title: Deutsch–Jozsa Algorithm
description: The Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm was the first to prove an exponential separation: it decides whether a binary function is constant or balanced with a single quantum query, where a classical computer needs 2^(n-1)+1 queries in the worst case. It has no practical use — but as a proof that quantum computers can be exponentially faster at something, it launched the field. One query versus millions is the cleanest demo of quantum parallelism ever found.

title: Quantum Walks
description: Quantum walks are the quantum analog of random walks, and they spread quadratically faster — hitting times drop from O(N) to O(√N) on many graphs. Childs showed they are universal for quantum computation, and walk-based algorithms give exponential speedups on glued-trees graphs and quadratic speedups for element distinctness. They model energy transport in photosynthesis, where quantum coherence may explain near-perfect efficiency.

title: Quantum Sensing and Metrology
description: Quantum sensing is the quantum technology already in the field: atomic clocks that lose a second in billions of years, magnetometers that image single neurons, gravimeters that find tunnels, all by pushing measurement to fundamental limits. Entangled sensors beat the shot-noise limit 1/√N and approach the Heisenberg limit 1/N. Unlike quantum computing, the advantage here is deployed, not promised.
